opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a funny tension, right? I'm someone who generally likes to have my hands on things. I'd rather understand exactly what's happening than delegate it and hope it works out. But scheduling is one of those tasks where the doing-it-yourself part isn't really where the value is. It's not like writing or thinking through a hard problem, where the process itself is how you figure out what you believe. Scheduling is just coordination overhead. It's a lot of back-and-forth, checking calendars, figuring out time zones, remembering that someone prefers mornings, rescheduling when something moves. None of that makes me smarter or better at my job.

So for me the line is: if doing it myself builds understanding or judgment, I want to do it. If it's pure logistics, I'm happy to hand it off. And an AI assistant is actually a pretty good fit there, because scheduling has a lot of structure. The constraints are mostly explicit, the preferences can be written down, and the cost of a small mistake is usually low and easy to fix.

There's also a control element that I think people underrate. With a human assistant you're often a step removed. You make a request and some time later it gets done. With an AI assistant I can see what it's proposing, tweak it, and approve it in a few seconds. So I still feel like I'm the one making the decisions; I'm just not doing the tedious part. That ends up matching how I like to work better than I expected.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls scheduling “coordination overhead” and “tedious,” but does not identify boredom with calendaring as Bob McGrew’s reason for delegating it.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, it's funny, because I'm the kind of person who really likes to have my hands on everything. I like knowing where my time is going, I like deciding what's worth it. So you'd think an assistant for scheduling would be exactly the thing I'd resist.

But scheduling isn't actually the part I care about. What I care about is the decision, like, do I want to take this meeting, is this the right week for it. The scheduling itself is just the tax you pay on that decision. It's eleven emails back and forth about whether Tuesday at two works, and then someone's in a different time zone, and then it moves. None of that is me doing the thing myself in any meaningful sense. It's me doing clerical work.

So the way I think about it is that an assistant doesn't take away my control, it actually gives me more of it. I still make the call about whether the meeting happens. I just don't spend the forty minutes of friction getting it onto the calendar. And honestly, that's what I think a lot of people get wrong about delegation generally, whether it's to a person or to an AI. The point isn't to stop caring about the details. It's to be very deliberate about which details are actually yours to own, and then be ruthless about handing off the rest.

r001.rationale: The response says scheduling is clerical work that creates friction, but it does not identify boredom with calendaring as Bob McGrew’s reason.
